evidence.title: Ramesuan (king of Ayutthaya)
evidence.text: Somdet Phra Ramesuan (Thai: สมเด็จพระราเมศวร ) (1339–1395), son of king Ramathibodi I, reigned as the second and fifth king of the kingdom of Ayutthaya.

evidence.title: Ramesuan (king of Ayutthaya)
evidence.text: When King Ramathibodi ascended to the throne of Ayuthaya, he sent King Ramesuan to reign in Lavo.

evidence.title: Ramesuan (king of Ayutthaya)
evidence.text: Upon King Ramathibodi's death in 1369, King Ramesuan traveled to Ayutthaya to assume the throne, but held it for less than a year before being deposed by his uncle, King Borommaracha I, the ruler of Suphanburi.

evidence.title: Ramesuan (king of Ayutthaya)
evidence.text: Sources differ over the nature of their conflict; official chronicles state that the older Boromaracha ruled with the willing consent of his nephew, while Jeremias van Vliet's "Short History of Thailand" indicated that Boromaracha's ascension came only after a bloody conflict bordering on civil war.

evidence.title: Minhlange
evidence.text: Minhlange (Burmese: မင်းလှငယ် , ] ; 1418–1425) was king of Ava for about three months in 1425.

evidence.title: Minhlange
evidence.text: Minhlange ascended to the throne in August 1425 after his father King Thihathu had been killed in an ambush by raiders from the Shan State of Hsipaw (Thibaw).

evidence.title: Minhlange
evidence.text: He was only about seven years old.

evidence.title: Minhlange
evidence.text: The ambush was arranged by Thihathu's powerful queen Shin Bo-Me who wanted to place her lover, Kale Kyetaungnyo, the Saopha of Kale, on the throne.

evidence.title: Minhlange
evidence.text: About three months later, Shin Bo-Me poisoned the young king in early November 1425 and made Kyetaungnyo king a few days later.

evidence.title: Harald V of Norway
evidence.text: Harald V (] ; born 21 February 1937) is the King of Norway, having ascended the throne following the death of his father on 17 January 1991.

evidence.title: MS Kronprins Harald
evidence.text: Several motor ships have borne the name Kronprins Harald, after Harald V of Norway:

evidence.title: Martanda Cinkaiariyan
evidence.text: Martanda Cinkaiariyan (Tamil: மார்த்தாண்ட சிங்கையாரியன் ) (died 1348) ascended the throne of Jaffna Kingdom under the throne name Pararasasekaram III.

evidence.title: Martanda Cinkaiariyan
evidence.text: He is one of the early Aryacakravarti kings about whom historical and epigraphical evidence is available.

evidence.title: Martanda Cinkaiariyan
evidence.text: He was noted by Ibn Battuta in his well-known travelogue as well as he has left behind a few inscriptions.

evidence.title: Martanda Cinkaiariyan
evidence.text: He oversaw the international trade of the Jaffna kingdom with Yemen via the kingdom's powerful trading ships.

evidence.title: Martanda Cinkaiariyan
evidence.text: Martanda Cinkaiariyan accompanied Battuta to the peak of "Sivanoli Padam Malai" along with Yogis and other Hindus and companions of the king who visited the sacred Shiva site annually.

evidence.title: Coloman, King of Hungary
evidence.text: Coloman the Learned, also the Book-Lover or the Bookish (Hungarian: "Könyves Kálmán" ; Croatian: "Koloman" ; Slovak: "Koloman Učený" ; 10703February 1116) was King of Hungary from 1095 and King of Croatia from 1097 until his death.

evidence.title: Coloman, King of Hungary
evidence.text: Because Coloman and his younger brother Álmos were underage when their father King Géza I of Hungary died, their uncle LadislausI ascended the throne in 1077.

evidence.title: Coloman, King of Hungary
evidence.text: Ladislaus prepared Colomanwho was "half-blind and humpbacked", according to late medieval Hungarian chroniclesfor a church career, and Coloman was eventually appointed bishop of Eger or Várad (Oradea, Romania) in the early 1090s.

evidence.title: Coloman, King of Hungary
evidence.text: The dying King Ladislaus preferred Álmos to Coloman when nominating his heir in early 1095.

evidence.title: Coloman, King of Hungary
evidence.text: Coloman fled from Hungary but returned around 19 July 1095 when his uncle died.

evidence.title: Coloman, King of Hungary
evidence.text: He was crowned in early 1096; the circumstances of his accession to the throne are unknown.

evidence.title: Coloman, King of Hungary
evidence.text: He granted the Hungarian Duchyone-third of the Kingdom of Hungaryto Álmos.

evidence.title: Parakrama Pandyan I
evidence.text: Parakrama Pandyan I was a Pandyan king of Tamilakkam, ruling from the Pandyan capital in Madurai.

evidence.title: Parakrama Pandyan I
evidence.text: He was besieged in a Pandyan war by his contemporary, rival and throne claimant Kulasekhara Pandyan in 1169, a vassal of the Chola Dynasty.

evidence.title: Parakrama Pandyan I
evidence.text: Parakrama Pandyan I sought assistance from the Ceylonese king Parakramabahu I of Polonnaruwa but was subsequently executed.

evidence.title: Parakrama Pandyan I
evidence.text: Kulasekhara Pandyan ascended to the Madurai throne but was eventually forced to seek refuge in Chola country in 1171.

evidence.title: Parakrama Pandyan I
evidence.text: Parakrama Pandyan I's son Vira Pandyan III ascended on the Pandyan throne before he was defeated by Chola forces.

evidence.title: Parakrama Pandyan I
evidence.text: In 1212 CE a succeeding namesake royal of the dynasty, Parakrama Pandyan II invaded Ceylon and became monarch at Polonnaruwa for three years with the title Parakrama Pandya of Polonnaruwa.

evidence.title: Lü Buwei
evidence.text: Lü Buwei (291–235 BC) was a politician of the Qin state in the Warring States period of ancient China.

evidence.title: Lü Buwei
evidence.text: Originally an influential merchant from the Wey (衛) state, Lü Buwei met and befriended King Zhuangxiang of Qin, who was then a minor prince serving as a hostage in the Zhao state.

evidence.title: Lü Buwei
evidence.text: Through bribes and machinations, Lü Buwei succeeded in helping King Zhuangxiang become the heir apparent to the Qin throne.

evidence.title: Lü Buwei
evidence.text: In 249 BC, after King Zhuangxiang ascended the throne following the death of his father, King Xiaowen, he appointed Lü Buwei as his chancellor (相國) and ennobled him as "Marquis Wenxin" (文信侯).

evidence.title: Lü Buwei
evidence.text: After King Zhuangxiang's death in 247 BC, Lü Buwei became the chancellor and regent to King Zhuangxiang's young son, Ying Zheng, who later became Qin Shi Huang (First Emperor of the Qin Dynasty).

evidence.title: Coenwulf of Mercia
evidence.text: Coenwulf (also spelled Cenwulf, Kenulf, or Kenwulph) was King of Mercia from December 796 until his death in 821.

evidence.title: Coenwulf of Mercia
evidence.text: He was a descendant of a sibling of King Penda, who had ruled Mercia in the middle of the 7th century.

evidence.title: Coenwulf of Mercia
evidence.text: He succeeded Ecgfrith, the son of Offa; Ecgfrith only reigned for five months, and Coenwulf ascended to the throne in the same year that Offa died.

evidence.title: Coenwulf of Mercia
evidence.text: In the early years of Coenwulf's reign he had to deal with a revolt in Kent, which had been under Offa's control.

evidence.title: Coenwulf of Mercia
evidence.text: Eadberht Præn returned from exile in Francia to claim the Kentish throne, and Coenwulf was forced to wait for papal support before he could intervene.

evidence.title: Coenwulf of Mercia
evidence.text: When Pope Leo agreed to anathematize Eadberht, Coenwulf invaded and retook the kingdom; Eadberht was taken prisoner, was blinded, and had his hands cut off.

evidence.title: Coenwulf of Mercia
evidence.text: Coenwulf also appears to have lost control of the kingdom of East Anglia during the early part of his reign, as an independent coinage appears under King Eadwald.

evidence.title: Coenwulf of Mercia
evidence.text: Coenwulf's coinage reappears in 805, indicating that the kingdom was again under Mercian control.

evidence.title: Coenwulf of Mercia
evidence.text: Several campaigns of Coenwulf's against the Welsh are recorded, but only one conflict with Northumbria, in 801, though it is likely that Coenwulf continued to support the opponents of the Northumbrian king Eardwulf.

evidence.title: Sen Soulintha
evidence.text: Sen Soulintha, Saen Surintha or Sen Sourintha (1511–1582) was born Chane Tian and became King of Lan Xang reigning 1571-1575 and again 1580-1582.

evidence.title: Sen Soulintha
evidence.text: Sen Soulintha was not of noble birth, rising from royal page to King Setthatirath’s Chief Minister.

evidence.title: Sen Soulintha
evidence.text: During the succession disputes in the Kingdom of Lan Na between King Setthatirath and King Mekuti, Sen Soulintha served Setthatirath as a general and successfully took several cities of Lan Na including Chiang Saen for which he was given the honorific name "Lusai" meaning “victory.”

evidence.title: Sen Soulintha
evidence.text: Sen Soulintha supported Setthatirath in leading the guerrilla campaigns during the Burmese invasions of King Bayinnaung.

evidence.title: Sen Soulintha
evidence.text: When Setthatirath died near Attapeu under suspicious circumstances in 1572, Sen Soulintha led the armies of Lan Xang back to Vientiane.

evidence.title: Sen Soulintha
evidence.text: A succession dispute erupted, which nearly led to civil war and provided a pretext for another Burmese invasion ordered by Bayinnaung and led by the Chief Minister Binnya Dala.

evidence.title: Sen Soulintha
evidence.text: Sen Soulintha defeated the Burmese and Lan Na forces led by Binnya Dala, an event which led to the latter’s exile, only to face a more massive invasion led by Bayinnaug the following year.

evidence.title: Sen Soulintha
evidence.text: Sen Soulintha again attempted to resort to guerilla tactics, but lacked popular support from his seizure of the throne.

evidence.title: Sen Soulintha
evidence.text: He and his son Ong Lo (Nakhon Noi) were captured by Bayinnaung and exiled to Pegu.

evidence.title: Sen Soulintha
evidence.text: The Burmese placed Setthathirath’s brother, and former "Ouphahat" or Viceroy, Prince Tha Heua on the throne.

evidence.title: Sen Soulintha
evidence.text: According to the Luang Prabang chronicles it was this brother, who had led a rebellion in Luang Prabang and tried to seize the throne from Setthathirath on the death of their father Photisarath.

evidence.title: Sen Soulintha
evidence.text: Prince Tha Heua took the regnal name Voravongsa and reigned under Burmese suzerainty from 1575-1579.

evidence.title: Sen Soulintha
evidence.text: Voravongsa was never popular, and drowned with his family while attempting to flee Vientiane in the face of popular uprising.

evidence.title: Sen Soulintha
evidence.text: In 1579, Bayinnaung dispatched a sizable army to restore order.

evidence.title: Sen Soulintha
evidence.text: According to Lao histories Sen Soulintha was then installed as king a second time in 1580.

evidence.title: Sen Soulintha
evidence.text: By that time Sen Soulintha was an old man and reigned only for two years before his son ascended the throne as Nakhon Noi and another succession dispute ensued.
